utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all of you; good afternoon, Office of the Prosecutor, the Defence; good afternoon, General Krstic. Madam Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-98-33-T, the Prosecutor versus Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We are here today for a Pre-Defence Conference envisaged in Rule 63 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We should first of all like to consider the points raised during the Status Conference of the 27th of September this year. In accordance with Rule 65 ter (G), the Defence has submitted a list of witnesses and a list of exhibits which it intends to offer in the course of the proceedings. A certain number of remarks were made by the Chamber and the Prosecutor regarding those lists, and the Defence pledged, in accordance with those comments, to comply with the provisions of Rule 65 ter (G) by the 4th of October, at the latest. Concerning the list of witnesses, the Defence took it upon itself to specify the status and function held by the witnesses which it intends to call, and specifically when those were members of the army of Republika Srpska, VRS, at the time of the facts. It also pledged to specify the counts in the indictment to which the testimony of the witnesses will refer. The Prosecutor also expressed the wish to be supplied with summaries, more detailed summaries, so that it might prepare adequately for the cross-examination. The Chamber noted regarding the latter point that the Prosecutor, unlike the Defence, does not have any witness statement. The Chamber, therefore, insisted in the name of the principle of the equality of arms on the necessity of the Defence complying as best it can to the provisions of Rule 65 ter (G), which the Defence accepted to do. As agreed, the Defence filed yesterday a completed list which specifies the rank and the positions held by military men who will be called as witnesses; also, the counts of the indictment to which the testimony will refer, and to a certain extent, the details regarding the contents of some of the testimonies. The question that now arises is, in the first place, to see whether the Prosecutor is satisfied with the level of precision provided. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon to my colleagues for the Defence. I received this document this morning. I was away yesterday, but it had been presented to my office yesterday and it was reviewed by both my colleagues and by myself. The answer to your question is that I am not satisfied in some particulars, and with the Court's permission, I will identify those areas, particularly, those witnesses where I believe there is not full compliance with Rule 65 ter. It has been our position in the past that merely identifying the topics about which a witness will testify and not providing the facts relating to that topic does not constitute full compliance with Rule 65 ter. In respect of Witness 22 and Witness 4, the summary that was provided to the Trial Chamber on the 14th of September, first starting with Witness 22, if the Trial Chamber has a copy of that document before it, the summary of Witness 22 is found on page 17. In the new submission that was filed on the 3rd of October, Witness 22 is found -- the summary is found on page 19. A comparison between the two summaries which, in the respectful submission of the Prosecutor, are topical submissions are virtually identical; there are no significant changes. In respect of Witness 4, and I direct the Court's attention to page 4 in both the 14 September pleading and the 3 October pleading where both summaries and submissions of the Defence are indicated, again I believe a comparison of the two reveal that what is contained is a topical summary, one; two, a summary that is virtually identical in the two submissions. And it is our respectful submission that the Trial Chamber find, (1) that these are virtually identical submissions; (2) that they are not factual submissions but topical submissions and that they do not comply with the Rule 65 ter. In that respect, Mr. President and Your Honours, we will be requesting that there be full compliance with the Rule, that is, that factual submissions be made in respect of those two witnesses, that they be made within five days, and that a failure to provide to the Office of the Prosecutor a complete factual summary of the testimonies of those witnesses will result in an order by this Chamber permitting the Office of the Prosecutor to identify -- I'm sorry, to interview those witnesses prior to their taking the stand and testifying. Now, let me direct the Court's attention to other areas where the Office of the Prosecutor is not satisfied, and I will start with Witness 9, the summary that is found -- his summary is found on page 8 of the most recent submission by the Defence, and I direct the Court's attention to the third paragraph in that submission, the last sentence. If I may be permitted to read that. The sentence reads as follows: "The witness will testify in the movement of General Krstic during the Operation Zepa until the end of this operation in late July 1995." Now, that's the topic about which this witness will testify, and from the Prosecutor's point of view, it is an important potential testimony because it identifies the locations of General Krstic and where he was and at what time he was at the various locations is an important and perhaps relevant consideration to any judgement that will be rendered in this case. Therefore, the Prosecution would request in that regard that there be facts that are submitted in respect of that particular portion of the summary, the topical summary, that has been submitted to this Chamber and to us. Now, I have two other examples that I will comment on, and both of those examples are found in the summary and the submission of the Defence in respect of Witness 14. My first comment is directed to a portion of the Defence submission found on page 13, and it is the third complete paragraph from the top of page 13 and it reads as follows: "The witness will testify on the takeover of duty of the commander" -- I'm sorry. Let me start that again: "The witness will testify on the takeover of duty of the commander of the Drina Corps between General Zivanovic and General Krstic." Now, that's the topic about which he'll testify, but the facts that will support that topic are not included in that summary under Rule 65. And clearly, as the Court knows, when General Krstic became the commander is a fundamental issue that the Court will have to decide in making any judgement in this case. So the Prosecutor's Office is requesting that there be a factual summary that will develop this topic about which this witness intends to testify. Turning to the paragraph directly above the paragraph which I have just read, it reads: "The witness will testify on the presence of General Zivanovic at the command post Vlasenica after the fall of Srebrenica." Again, the topic is identified but the facts are absent. The facts such as the date, the time, the circumstances are, in fact, missing, and this is not very helpful for us in terms of permitting us to prepare a proper cross-examination. Our request in respect of those paragraphs and these two witnesses that I have identified are the same, that within five calendar days, the Defence provide to the Office of the Prosecutor and to the Trial Chamber factual summaries that relate to the paragraphs that I have identified, and, further, that in the absence of a proper submission, proper factual submission, the Office of the Prosecutor be permitted to interview these witnesses prior to their testifying before the Trial Chamber on these topics. The next point -- and I will say for the record I've had an opportunity to talk to my colleagues from the Defence on this next point -- in fact, all of the points I've raised with Your Honours and I'm raising now. I explained to the Defence that in respect of Witnesses 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 17, the submission -- the most recent submission of the Defence identifies, and I quote, "This Infantry Battalion," without identifying which specific Infantry Battalion each of these individuals was a member of. Now, I have been informed by the Defence now of that particular Infantry Battalion, and I would ask that for the record, they identify the Infantry Battalions to which these individuals belong. They're prepared to do so, and then we will have a fully developed record in respect of this point that we are raising. Now, in many of these instances, Mr. President and Your Honours, there is no rank provided for these individuals, and our request is that in order to fully flesh out the biographical data that would permit us to prepare for this examination, the rank of these individuals, if it is known and if it is available to the Defence, that information be provided to us. My last comment is directed to a portion of the Defence submission in respect of Witness 18, and I am referring to page 16 of the most recent submission. About two-thirds down on that page for Witness 18 is found the following sentence, and it relates to General Mladic, and I quote: "He will testify about the arrival of General Mladic and his speech delivered to the soldiers." Now, the role of General Mladic, as the Trial Chamber is aware, is something that is very important in this case. While I understand that Witness 18 will testify about a speech, I don't know if this speech bears on the issues before this Trial Chamber or is a speech, for example, that would merely be a speech saying to his subordinate troops, "Good job, you've done an excellent job," or something to boost their morale. My request is that that topic be developed in a factual sense in order to comply with Rule 65 ter. Those are my remarks, Mr. President and Your Honours, in respect of this most recent submission by the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I followed you for the most part, but I did have the following question: As to Witness 4, who is only going to testify, I gather, about the events leading up to the events here; namely, until the fall of Srebrenica - apparently he's not going to testify, as far as I can see, about the period or the events that we're most concerned with - do you really need that same level of detail? I understand your later points; they're critical. But we've heard all kinds of testimony about all the events that lead up. I just want to know how specific you need that kind of background testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My answer is it's less important, Your Honour, than the other items that I've mentioned. However, to the extent that specific locations are mentioned, I do have information about events that took place in respect of locations, I would like to have those locations, for example, identified. I may wish to present those contradicting facts to the witness. But in answer to your question, in the general sense, it's less important than the other items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we have at least three groups of remarks that were given by the Prosecutor. We should, of course, also like to hear the view of the Defence regarding the remarks that were made by the Prosecutor. Mr. Petrusic, I think that during the last Status Conference we somehow mentioned the possibility to discuss these issues in a theoretical manner, but I do not wish to have a theoretical discussion at this point. However, there is one thing that needs to be clarified and made specific before you give us your response. If we say that it is enough for the Prosecutor to say that the witnesses will come to testify about paragraph such and such of the indictment, it is also possible for the Prosecutor to tell the Defence that the witness in question will come and testify about the relevant paragraph. So as regards Rule 65 ter and its provisions, subrule (G) - yes, I think that that is the relevant provision - the provision speaks about the summary of the facts on which each witness will testify. I think that the wording "summary of the facts" refers to circumstances; what the witness is actually going to talk about, when the events happened, why, where, and so on and so forth. So I believe that the facts have to be specified in terms of description of the events. That is something that I wanted to say before Mr. Petrusic gives his response. So what is the view of the Defence, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours; good afternoon, Mr. President. The Defence is not going to engage in any theoretical discussion. We will try to be as specific as possible in our response to the comments that were made by the counsel for the Prosecution. I think that once our arguments have been entered into the record things will be sufficiently clear. As regards Witness 4, the Defence will probably forego his testimony during this case because in the meantime it has obtained certain documents which might substitute the testimony of the witness. And the documents of course will be made available to the Prosecutor as soon as possible. As regards the comment which was made in respect of Witness 14 and the paragraphs referred to by my learned colleague from the Prosecution, I shall like to note for the record that the witness will be speaking about the fact that the takeover of duty between General Zivanovic and General Krstic, the duty of the commander of the Drina Corps, took place on the 20th or the 21st of July, in the vicinity of Han Pijesak. Secondly, as regards the second remark which was made in respect of this witness, the Defence will clarify the matter by saying that the witness will be speaking about the fact that General Zivanovic, on his command post in Vlasenica -- that he was at his command post in Vlasenica also on the 13th, the 14th, and also after the 15th of July. Likewise, the Defence will also try to respond to the comment which was made in respect of Witness 9 by stating the fact that the same witness was in charge of security of General Krstic, that he was actually chief of his security personnel; that on the 13th of July and later, until the 2nd of August, General Krstic's whereabouts were within combat lines in the theatre in Zepa, in the area of Zepa; that he travelled to those lines by car as far as it was possible in view of the inaccessibility of certain portions of the terrain. As regards the testimony of Witness 18 and the comment made in respect of that witness, we should like to say that that witness will testify about General Mladic's address to the group of soldiers, amongst whom was also the witness, one day after the fall of Srebrenica. The witness will also say that General Mladic told him that they would immediately be going to Zepa. I can accept the remark of my learned colleague made in respect of Witness 22. The Defence did not have contact with that witness. However, we have information to the effect that the witness in question was heard as a witness in the case which is before the Public Prosecutor's Office in Banja Luka. And also bearing in mind facts that have so far been heard during the proceedings, that is, that the witness in question is an officer of Republika Srpska, in particular the officer of the Drina Corps or was an officer of the Drina Corps during the relevant times, and also bearing in mind the fact that his name was mentioned on a number of times, the Defence believes that for the purposes of ascertaining the truth and all the relevant facts, his testimony would be relevant for this particular case. I must admit that his testimony, for the time being, is somewhat a mystery for the Defence at this point in time. But I also must say that I believe that every individual, especially an officer of the Drina Corps whose name was mentioned on a number of occasions so far in this case, would probably have a lot to say in terms of facts in respect of almost all of the counts of the indictment and the paragraphs of the indictment in general. Lastly, when this comes to the identification of Witnesses 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 17, I should like to ask the Trial Chamber to move into private session for this part of the debate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Rodrigues, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Mr. Petrusic, you are asking a private session because you will be mentioning the identity of potentially protected witnesses or persons. Is that the reason for your request?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason I'm applying for a private session is only for the purposes of identification of the unit to which they belonged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. We'll move into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Petrusic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this has been more or less our position regarding the comments that were made by the Prosecutor. I don't know whether this is enough for the Prosecutor and the Chamber. If not, we still have the possibility which was mentioned by Mr. Harmon, that is, that within the next five days, working days, we disclose the relevant document, we provide the relevant documents. However, we believe that we have fully complied with the provisions of Rule 65 ter (G). I owe you an apology, Mr. President, an apology to both the Chamber and my colleagues from the Prosecution, because we have certain difficulties when it comes to the technical side of this procedure. We Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have provided you only with numbers of witnesses, but in the meantime, the Registry has been provided with a full copy of the document, including the names of witnesses whom we intend to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. I should like to hear the position of Mr. Harmon once again. The question that is before us is the following: Are the documents sufficient, the documents that are before us, including the information that we have just heard, or do we still need a time period of five days for additional information so that the Prosecution may be able to appropriately conduct its cross-examinations? Mr. Harmon, can we hear you once again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And thank you to my colleague. Certainly in respect to Witness 4 where my colleague says they will probably forego the testimony, we need additional guidance. Do they intend to forego the testimony of that witness? In which case, there is no need for a factual summary. If they do intend to proceed with the testimony of Witness 4, then we would request an additional summary that is in compliance with Rule 65. In respect of the last submission of my colleague, that is, the units to which Witnesses 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 17 belong, we're satisfied with that submission and would not request any additional submissions by the Defence. In respect of the comments of my colleague relating to Witness 18, if the substance of the speech by General Mladic is as described by my colleague, we will not require and do not require any additional submissions. In respect, however, of Witness 14, the two items that have been described and commented upon by my colleague, and in respect of Witness 9, we believe that additional factual summaries -- a more robust factual summary is required for us to adequately prepare our cross-examination, and we would make a request for an additional factual summary within five days. I believe that addresses all of the comments. Perhaps not. On Witness 22 -- if I may have just a minute. Witness 22, we believe that an additional factual summary must be submitted, and we would make a request that that submission be prepared within five days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can understand, in respect of Witness 22 and Witnesses 9 and 14, it seems that Mr. Harmon is requesting additional information, additional facts, and a more robust summary. As regards Witness 4, if he is going to be called, additional facts are also necessary. As regards Witness 18, if the content of the speech is confirmed, then the Prosecutor will not need any additional information. I think that your task has been significantly facilitated, Mr. Petrusic. As regards Witnesses 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 17, the Prosecutor seems to be happy with the additional information that you have just provided; I don't think that you have any additional work to do. Do you wish to comment, or do you still accept the delay of five days?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Petrusic. As regards this item, I believe that we have already agreed. Mr. Petrusic, you have been granted an additional five days to supply the Prosecutor with the information he requested. There is one more item on the agenda that needs to be discussed, and that is the list of exhibits. Concerning the list of exhibits, the Defence has not submitted to the Chamber any new list. During our last Status Conference, the Prosecutor deplored the insufficiency of information contained in the list. In his opinion, the information was not sufficient enough for him to be able to authenticate the documents that were contained, as is required by the provisions of Rule 65 ter (G)(ii). The Chamber wishes, therefore, to know whether the parties have been able to meet and discuss this particular issue, and whether they have been able to reach an agreement. The Defence took it upon itself to provide the Prosecutor with sources that they intend to use. This is just a preliminary issue, preliminary question. Let me first of all find out if you have managed to reach an agreement before the Status Conference. Afterwards, we have three items to discuss: Has any additional information been provided, and is it sufficient? Did the Prosecutor request any documents containing relevant sources, and have such documents been provided? Are there any disputes as regards authenticity of the documents which are contained in the list of the Defence? So these are the issues that the Chamber believes need to be addressed so that the case can properly be prepared. Let me first of all give the floor to Mr. Visnjic, and then after that to the Prosecutor, if you agree with that Mr. Harmon. Mr. Visnjic, how come we still don't have the list of exhibits? That is the first question, and that is why I gave you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as regards the exhibits, the Defence respected the dynamics of the submission of exhibits that was used during the case for the Prosecution. There are certain documents which we termed as key military documents, and the Defence does not have such documents. We were provided those documents from the Prosecutor within a certain period of time which was acceptable by both parties. So the Defence will be using the same documents, that is, the military documents, during its case, and they will be provided to the Prosecutor. As regards the documentation, we provided the list of books, titles of books, that the Defence will be mentioning during their part of the case, and we do not have any other specific or special exhibits as regards that area. We will be using the exhibits that were already tendered by the Prosecutor during the presentation of their evidence. As regards photographs, any photographs that we might use, if we are going to use them, they will be tendered into evidence prior to the testimony, as it was done by the Prosecutor. However, I think that there will be very few. We didn't specifically discuss this issue with the Prosecutor, because we believed that we had already reached an agreement regarding documents. I don't know if my learned colleague Mr. Harmon has anything else to add. We are ready to hear him on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have heard the Defence. The Defence is at your disposal. You may take advantage of it, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I explained earlier, the Defence and the Prosecution have an agreement in respect of key military documents, and I'm satisfied by the terms of that agreement that we will have sufficient time in which to determine authentication issues. I can't comment on any authentication issue at the moment because I have not been presented with any single document. I confirm certainly what my colleague has indicated to the Chamber, that shortly before we commenced this proceeding, my colleagues handed to me a list of books, the titles of books that they intend to rely upon in their submissions, and I have that. And they have indicated to me that they will be assisting me if I need the translation of that document, which is in B/C/S, and I thank them for that. Certainly if they're going to rely upon the documents that have been presented by the Office of the Prosecutor, we will have no objection to the authentication of any of those exhibits. We believe they are authentic in the first instance. That's why we offered them. I have no comments in respect of the photographs because, as I understand, there will be very few. And to the extent that my colleagues wish to divulge those before they are tendered into evidence, we are certainly available to see them. In respect of the situation that we had in the presentation of the Prosecution evidence, we did make prior disclosure of photographs, at least of some photographs, to the Defence, but again, I think throughout this procedure the parties have respected the equality of arms principle and will continue to do so during this proceeding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Harmon, can I conclude from what you've said that there's no problem regarding this item of a list of exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. Very good. Thank you. There is perhaps another minor point. Is the Defence in a position today to indicate more or less when, on what date, you will be able to submit the expert reports? If you have any indication of that, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as we stated earlier on in our case, we will be presenting the findings of two expert witnesses, a pathologist and a military expert. Immediately prior to leaving, I received a draft of the report by the pathologist, and I assume that in the course of next week, we will receive the final report which we will have translated immediately. I think that the report of the military expert will be ready within a period of ten days. And all that remains for us to do, which I consider to be a problem, is the problem of translation. But I will be having a meeting immediately after this conference with the registrar so that I hope we will be able to overcome that problem. As we reported earlier, we will submit the pathologist report immediately to the registrar in the Serbian version, and, of course, once the translation is ready, we will be disclosing it in English as well. As for the military expert, his report will be disclosed 21 days prior to his testimony, as provided for by the Rules. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Harmon, have you any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have none, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think there's also the question of timetable. As you know, six weeks for the Defence case divided into two sessions were stipulated in the schedule, and this is actually equal to 25 hearing days. At our Status Conference, I said 30. I hesitated between 30 and 25. It is true that it is a question of six weeks, but there are a few days when we will not be sitting, so that in reality, it will be 25 days of hearings. According to the list of witnesses submitted in accordance with Rule 65 ter (G), the Defence envisaged some 23 days required for the examination of the 25 witnesses they intend to call. Mr. Petrusic now tells us that it may not be 25 but 24. Is the Prosecutor able to indicate the time he thinks he will need for the cross-examination of those witnesses and, of course, the cross-examination of the accused? Have the parties had occasion, time -- had occasion to discuss the possibility of reducing the time needed? The Chamber believes that once there is testimony, and I must concede to Mr. Petrusic what he said at the last Status Conference, but even if there is some repetition, the Chamber may cut it short or the Chamber may speed things up. We already know this. This is an optimistic forecast, of course. Perhaps we might be able to shorten a little the time that you have envisaged. But regardless of that, I would like to know whether the time that you have planned, whether that is an optimistic or a pessimistic forecast. Were you generous or more restrained in your estimates? So I'm going to ask Mr. Visnjic or Mr. Petrusic about this and then I'll come to the Prosecution and the time they need for the cross-examination. And, of course, the other question: Whether the parties have done anything in terms of trying to shorten the time needed for the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination. We spoke at the previous Status Conference of the need to contact Madam Registrar. She indicated her availability and readiness to help in facilitating in whatever way possible the process of dealing with exhibits and wasting as little time as possible. So, Mr. Petrusic, was your estimate an optimistic or a pessimistic one? If I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would say that I could group the witnesses into three categories when it comes to time. The Defence, for one group of witnesses, and I will list them, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 17, the Defence will indeed try to shorten the time for their testimony then envisaged, and it will indeed be shorter, so that my learned friends from the Prosecution will probably also not need long for the cross-examination. Then comes the second group of witnesses which includes officers of the army of Republika Srpska, the officers of the former Drina Corps. They will be reduced to realistic frameworks of the estimated time, and of course we will do our best during the examination not to abuse the time allotted to us by the Chamber. Finally, I would say that the Defence, in quotation marks - please don't misinterpret me - will not save time when it comes to the testimony of General Krstic. Of course, I'm not saying that we will waste time, but simply we consider this testimony to be of key importance. After all, he is the accused in this case, and the Defence is duty-bound to respect that. Therefore, to sum up, my forecast is an optimistic one, and in any event we will certainly fit within the time of six weeks to conclude our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon. Excuse me, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. What would be a realistic framework of time? You said for the second group it would be a realistic framework of time. What do you term "realistic"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the time envisaged in our submission, that is, the time that we have estimated already in our brief. If necessary, I can look it up and give you an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, if you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, if indeed the calculation is that of the 25 days that the Court envisions hearing the remainder of this case, 23 of those days are devoted to the direct examination of the Defence witnesses, I can say with great confidence that we will take more than two days to cross-examine these witnesses. I envision perhaps a three-day cross-examination of General Krstic. And in respect of the witnesses in the categories that have been identified by my colleagues, certainly depending on the rank and the position of the witness, perhaps but it's not necessarily certain, the examination will be more extensive. In respect of the officers of the Drina Corps, I think the examinations of those witnesses will be robust, but certainly an examination within an eye toward efficiency. When we get to the first category of witnesses, that is, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 17, since those witnesses appear to be quite repetitious in the subject matter about which they will be testifying, I can envision diminished amounts of time required for the cross-examination of those witnesses. But I will say that I do believe without any reservation that our cross-examination of these witnesses will take at a minimum two weeks, that is, all of these witnesses. I say that and I'm in the realm of pure speculation, because I haven't heard the testimonies of these witnesses and it's difficult to make proper calculations based on the witness summaries that we have been provided. But I think it's a fair assessment that at a minimum the Prosecutor will require two weeks. That's our submission, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that our estimate was extremely optimistic in the final analysis. For the moment, perhaps we should leave things as they stand, and after the first week we will perhaps be in a position to say what is, in fact, going to happen and whether we need some additional time. We would choose either to convene additional sessions, for example, in the afternoon, so as to be able to abide by the schedule, because as you know the Chamber has other cases in its programme; or we will review the whole schedule of the Chamber to allot more time so as to have normal conditions. For the moment, we will keep our schedule as it stands. After the first week, perhaps we will be in a position to review the conditions and to make the necessary adjustments in the schedule. There's another matter connected to the timetable, but before talking about that, I should like to confer with my colleagues, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the second point that I should like to address with you is the actual working hours, daily working hours. As you know, we have been working with our working hours beginning at 9.30, going on until 2.30 in the afternoon, 2.30 p.m. There have been many requests from several sides to have a longer break in order for people to be able to have lunch. People were complaining that the President was harassing people working in the chamber, making them work during the lunch hour. I wish to say that the President was very much aware of this because he needs that time too. So what we have decided, and what we would like to propose to you and also to communicate to you, is that we're going to begin at 9.20 and finish at 3.00. I think such a timetable has already been distributed; I believe so but I will check with Madam Registrar. Before doing that, I would like to say the following: There will be a half-hour break, the first break, and the second break will be of one hour, which means that previously we had four hours of sitting, effective four hours; now we will have more time. We'll have four hours and ten minutes, and the advantage also being that we will be able to have lunch. So I think this is quite fair to adopt a timetable which will not only allow us to have lunch and eat but also to work more. So as I have told you, this is both a communication and a proposition. So I'm going to ask Madam Registrar to see whether such a timetable has already been communicated and distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. The timetable was distributed, I believe, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to hear the reaction of the parties. Mr. Harmon, are you satisfied by having a little time for lunch?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are, Mr. President. My staff is as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Defence. Mr. Petrusic? Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are satisfied with this timetable, but we would like to draw the attention of the Chamber to the fact that during the testimony of General Krstic, we might need to adjust the timetable a little in view of his health. So we might perhaps suggest that we have a couple of brief breaks within the global timetable you have proposed. So that applies only to the time when General Krstic will be called to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will bear that in mind, and you were quite right drawing our attention to this, because we were going to consult General Krstic, but you spoke on his behalf. We have the necessary information, and we'll act accordingly. There is one thing that we need to do. Due to engagements accepted earlier, instead of beginning these hearings on the 16th of October, we're going to begin on the 18th [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Wald tells me that there seems to be a problem with the transcript. What I said was that we're going to begin the hearings for the Defence to begin its case on the 16th, the 16th of October, but the timetable we were discussing is not going to come into force on the 16th but on the 18th, which is to say that on the 16th and the 17th, we will be working from 9.30 until 2.30 p.m., according to the same timetable we had before. After the 18th, after the 18th, we will be beginning with the new timetable, which means that we will begin hearings at 9.20 in the morning and concluding at 3.00 p.m. in the afternoon. Is that clear now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be even more precise, on the 17th, the 17th, we will not finish at 2.30 but at 2.00 p.m. Someone has just reminded me of another commitment we have. So to sum up, on the 16th, we will be sitting from 9.30 until 2.30 p.m.; on the 17th, we will be sitting from 9.30 until 2.00 p.m.; on the 18th, we will begin with the new timetable, which means the sittings begin at 9.20 and finish at 3.00 p.m. So I think that now it's clear, and I think that we have no other matters to address except if the parties have anything else to communicate or to observe, or to raise regarding the opening of the Defence case, the opening of this stage of the proceedings, I must add. Mr. Harmon, is that all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Chamber, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has nothing more to raise either, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So that ends the Pre-Defence Conference. We wish you success in your work in the meantime, for almost another week, and then we will meet again here on the 16th of October. So good evening to you all.
